SLOOS-informed adjustment to the assessment:
- Credit supply and demand: Banks broadly eased lending standards across C&I and CRE (including construction, land development, nonfarm nonresidential, and multifamily) and reported stronger C&I loan demand from large, middle-market, and small firms, along with more credit line inquiries. Reasons cited include improved economic outlook, competition, higher risk tolerance, ample liquidity, and solid capital positions. This corroborates the FOMC’s statement that financial conditions remain accommodative and that the flow of credit to businesses is supportive of growth.
- Consumer and housing cross-currents: Despite easing for several consumer products (credit cards, autos, HELOCs, jumbo, and non-QM), banks expect deterioration in household credit (especially credit cards, autos, and nonconforming jumbos) in 2022 and reported weaker demand for residential real estate loans (including GSE-eligible and subprime). This tempers the positive impulse and aligns with an anticipated rise in interest rates.
- Policy alignment: SLOOS expectations for higher rates and improving business loan performance are consistent with the FOMC’s planned liftoff and taper conclusion, suggesting near-term resilience in business credit with prospective headwinds for household credit as policy tightens.

Net tone: More supportive than a macro-only read due to broad easing and stronger business loan demand, but moderated by expected household-credit deterioration and softer mortgage demand as rates rise.
